title: Commercial Solar ROI: How to Calculate Payback for Your Business
excerpt: Before signing a commercial solar contract, here's how to run the numbers yourself — and what most installers won't volunteer upfront.
body:
Buying a commercial solar system is a capital investment, not just an energy bill reducer. Yet many business owners sign contracts based on a single payback figure their installer calculated. Running your own numbers — or at least understanding how they're built — protects you from over-promising and helps you compare quotes fairly.

## Why Commercial Solar ROI Is More Complex Than Residential

A home system is simple: you generate power, you use it or export it. A commercial system involves:

- **Higher load variability** — factories, cold stores, and offices consume power very differently across shifts and seasons
- **Demand tariff components** — many commercial electricity accounts include a separate demand charge based on peak 15- or 30-minute usage, which solar may not reduce
- **Depreciation and tax treatment** — businesses can depreciate solar assets, which changes the real after-tax cost
- **Feed-in tariff limitations** — commercial feed-in rates in most states are low (often 3–8 c/kWh), so self-consumption is where the value is

Ignoring any one of these can make a good system look great — or a mediocre one look acceptable.

## Step 1: Establish Your Actual Self-Consumption Rate

Self-consumption is the share of solar generation your business actually uses on-site, rather than exporting. A system that runs while your building is occupied and powered up might achieve 70–85% self-consumption. A warehouse that's closed on weekends might manage 40%.

Ask your installer to show the self-consumption estimate and the assumptions behind it. If they can't, that's a red flag.

**Rule of thumb:** Every percentage point of self-consumption that shifts from export to on-site use can be worth 20–30 c/kWh more in value (buying at retail rather than selling at feed-in rates).

## Step 2: Build a Simple Payback Calculation

The basic formula:

| Input | Where to get it |
|---|---|
| System cost after incentives (AUD) | Installer quote minus STC value |
| Annual energy savings (AUD) | Self-consumed kWh × retail tariff |
| Annual export revenue (AUD) | Exported kWh × feed-in tariff |
| Annual O&M costs (AUD) | Monitoring, cleaning, inverter reserve |

**Simple payback (years) = Net system cost ÷ (Annual savings + Export revenue − O&M costs)**

For a 100 kW system costing $120,000 after STCs, generating $28,000 in annual savings and $3,000 in export revenue with $1,500 in O&M costs, simple payback is:

$120,000 ÷ ($28,000 + $3,000 − $1,500) = **4.1 years**

Simple payback doesn't account for the time value of money. For a more rigorous view, ask for an NPV or IRR calculation using a discount rate that reflects your cost of capital (typically 6–10% for Australian businesses in 2026).

## Step 3: Account for Depreciation and Tax

Australian businesses can claim solar systems as a depreciable asset. Depending on your circumstances and the current instant asset write-off thresholds, the effective after-tax cost of the system may be meaningfully lower than the sticker price. Speak to your accountant before signing — this can shift your payback by a year or more.

## Step 4: Stress-Test the Key Assumptions

Most installer proposals use optimistic inputs. Before you accept a payback figure, ask:

- **What retail tariff did you assume?** If they used your current rate without accounting for the fact that tariffs may change, the model is fragile.
- **What degradation rate did you apply?** Solar panels lose roughly 0.5–0.7% of output per year. A 10-year model should reflect this.
- **Is demand charge reduction included?** If yes, how was it calculated? Demand savings are real but harder to guarantee.
- **What happens if self-consumption drops?** Ask for a sensitivity scenario at 20% lower self-consumption.

## Common Mistakes That Inflate ROI Projections

- Using peak retail tariff rates without accounting for time-of-use pricing
- Omitting inverter replacement costs (central inverters often need replacement within 10–15 years)
- Assuming feed-in tariffs remain constant over the system's life
- Calculating payback on gross system cost rather than net-of-STC cost (or vice versa, inconsistently)
- Not modelling the impact of future load changes — if your business grows or shifts hours, generation and consumption patterns change

## Actionable Takeaway

Before you approve any commercial solar proposal, build your own payback spreadsheet using the inputs above and run two scenarios: an optimistic case (installer's numbers) and a conservative case (reduce self-consumption by 15%, increase O&M by 20%, and apply 0.6% annual degradation). If the conservative case still delivers payback under seven years, the project is likely worth pursuing. If only the optimistic case works, negotiate harder or walk away.
